notes.meaning: A man named Elkanah lived in the hill country of Ephraim. Although he lived in the land of Ephraim, his family record shows he was a Levite, belonging to the tribe chosen for sacred work. God began the story of Israel's great spiritual renewal not with a king, but with an ordinary, faithful family.

Elkanah had two wives, named Hannah and Peninnah. Having more than one wife was common at that time, but it went against God's original plan for marriage and brought constant strife into homes. Peninnah had sons and daughters, while Hannah carried the deep sorrow of having no children.

Every year, Elkanah traveled to the tabernacle at Shiloh to worship God and offer sacrifices. This is the first place in Scripture where God is given the title the LORD of Hosts, meaning the Lord over all the armies of heaven and earth. Even though Eli's two sons were serving as corrupt priests there, Elkanah still remained faithful to public worship.

When Elkanah presented his peace offering at Shiloh, he received back meat to share with his family as a shared meal before God. He gave portions of the sacred feast to Peninnah and to each of her sons and daughters. This family meal was meant to be a joyful time of thanksgiving together.

Elkanah gave Hannah a double portion of the sacrifice to show how deeply he loved her. Even though the Lord had kept her from having children, Elkanah's affection for her never changed. Hannah's barrenness was hard to bear, yet it was part of God's hidden purpose to prepare her for something greater.

Peninnah took advantage of Hannah's empty arms to mock and upset her year after year. She was jealous of Elkanah's deep love for Hannah, so she used Hannah's childlessness as a weapon to make her miserable. This cruel teasing added heavy emotional pain to Hannah's silent heartbreak.

This cruel badgering happened every single year when they traveled up to the house of the Lord. Instead of enjoying the sacred feast, Hannah was reduced to bitter tears and could not bring herself to eat. God's law forbade eating holy food while in deep mourning, so Hannah had to step aside in grief.

Elkanah saw his wife weeping and asked why she was grieving and refusing to eat. He kindly asked if his own tender love for her was not better to her than ten sons. Though his words were well-meant, he did not understand that a husband's affection could never remove a woman's longing to be a mother.

After they had finished their meal at Shiloh, Hannah rose quietly to go and pray. Eli the high priest was sitting in his seat by the entrance of the sanctuary. While Eli watched the courtyard, Hannah sought out a quiet place to lay her sorrow before the Lord.

Hannah was crushed in spirit, weeping openly as she prayed before the Lord. She did not trade insults with Peninnah or hide her pain from God, but poured out her raw feelings in His presence. Believers can always bring their deepest sorrows directly to God in honest prayer.

Hannah made a solemn vow, asking the LORD of Hosts to notice her misery and grant her a son. She promised that if God gave her a male child, she would dedicate him to the Lord for his whole life instead of just the normal years of Levitical service. She also promised that no razor would touch his head, devoting him as a lifelong Nazirite, someone entirely separated to God's work.

Hannah lingered before the Lord, praying silently for a long time. Her prayer was so earnest and prolonged that Eli the priest kept his eyes fixed on her mouth. Scripture often records only the heart of a prayer when a godly person pours out soul-deep petitions.

Hannah was speaking only in her heart, so while her lips moved, no sound came out of her mouth. Because silent prayer was unusual and her body trembled with emotion, Eli assumed she was drunk from the festival wine. God hears the quiet desires of our hearts even when no words can be heard out loud.

Eli confronted Hannah harshly and told her to stop being drunken and to put away her wine. His hasty assumption showed how corrupt the sanctuary had become, since drunkenness was apparently a common sight at the feasts. Spiritual leaders need to be careful not to judge people's motives before hearing the truth.

Hannah answered Eli with great respect, calling him 'my lord' rather than answering back in anger. She told him that she had drunk neither wine nor beer, but was an afflicted woman pouring out her inner sorrow before the Lord. She explained that her unusual behavior came from a broken heart, not from alcohol.

Hannah pleaded with Eli not to view her as a wicked or worthless woman. She told him that her moving lips came entirely from the overflow of her anguish and misery. When we are misunderstood, answering with gentleness and honesty is always the best response.

Eli quickly recognized his error and sent Hannah away with a blessing of peace. As God's priest, he prayed that the God of Israel would grant the petition she had asked of Him. God used Eli's encouraging pastoral word to give Hannah fresh hope.

Hannah thanked Eli and asked for his continued kindness and prayers. She then went on her way, ate her food with a comforted heart, and her face was no longer sad. Even before seeing the answer with her own eyes, she believed God's promise and found true relief.

Early the next morning, the family rose to worship the Lord before making their journey back to Ramah. After they returned home, Elkanah was intimate with Hannah, and the Lord remembered her plea. God never forgets His people, but remembering means He stepped forward to answer her prayer.

Hannah conceived and gave birth to a son just as she had hoped. She named the baby Samuel, which sounds like the Hebrew words for 'asked of God' and 'heard by God.' Every time his name was spoken, it stood as a joyful witness to God's faithfulness in answering prayer.

When the time arrived for the yearly festival, Elkanah took his household up to Shiloh to offer sacrifices and fulfill his vow. His own vow shows that he had fully supported Hannah's prayer and had made his own sacred promises regarding the child. He led his home by putting worship and obedience to God first.

Hannah chose to stay at home until she had weaned the little boy. She explained to Elkanah that once Samuel was weaned, she would bring him to Shiloh so he could remain in the Lord's service permanently. Caring for a young child at home is sacred work that pleases God just as much as attending public worship.

Elkanah gave his full blessing to Hannah's plan and urged her to do whatever seemed best to her. He prayed that the Lord would confirm His word and watch over the child until his service began. A godly home flourishes when husband and wife support each other in keeping promises made to God.

Once the boy was weaned, around three years old, Hannah traveled up to Shiloh with him. She brought generous offerings, including a bull for sacrifice, a large measure of flour, and wine for a drink offering. Although Samuel was still very young, she brought him to God's house to begin his lifelong calling.

After the bull was slaughtered as a burnt offering, the parents brought the young boy to Eli the priest. The slain sacrifice dedicated the living child to God for sacred service at the sanctuary. Hannah freely placed her most treasured earthly blessing into the Lord's hands.

Hannah introduced herself to Eli and reminded him that she was the very woman who had stood beside him weeping and praying years earlier. She did not bring up his past harsh words or hold a grudge against him. Instead, she pointed to herself simply as living proof of God's mercy.

Hannah showed the little boy to Eli and declared that this child was the answer to her desperate prayers. The Lord had heard her humble cry and given her exactly what she requested. When God answers our prayers, we should openly give Him the praise and tell others what He has done.

Hannah dedicated Samuel to the Lord for the rest of his days, explaining that because he was asked of God, he was now given back to God. She kept her solemn vow completely, holding nothing back from the Lord who had blessed her. Right there in the sanctuary, they all bowed down and worshiped God together.
